observations.exclusion_reason: TOOL ARTIFACT, not a property of this window: lib/git.js computes each commit's stats with `git show --numstat --format="" <sha>`, which for a two-parent merge diffs against the first parent by default. For a single-commit PR merged via GitHub's 'Merge pull request' button, that reproduces the exact diff of the merge's sole child commit, so the same real-world change is counted twice in the 50-commit sample as if it were two independent commits. In this window 10 of the 50 analyzed commits are such merges, and 6 of them exactly duplicate a sibling commit's (additions, deletions, files_changed) signature -- e.g. 26071400 'Merge pull request #21542' and a5936755 'Deprecate Evented...' both show (1080, 286, 30) -- so 12/50 (24%) of the sample double-counts 6 real changes. Not fixed here per instructions (measurement only); flagged as a new tool defect for repos with true merge-commit history. observations.notes: message_quality_pct scored 0/50: CONFIG's quality heuristic requires a Conventional-Commits prefix (feat:/fix:/etc, which git.git's 'component: summary' subject style does not use, e.g. 'mailmap: map Elijah Newren's current and previous work addresses' is not conventional-commit-shaped) OR >=10 words in the subject line alone (scoreMessageQuality is only ever given the git-log '%s' subject, never the body). Git's own CONTRIBUTING documentation explicitly asks for a short subject with the explanation in the body -- exactly the style this heuristic scores as low-quality. This is a construct-validity concern with message_quality_pct itself, not a bug in this run, but it means the metric conflates 'long/conventional subject line' with 'well-explained commit,' which will systematically penalize any project (git, and likely postgres, and the Linux-kernel-style C world generally) that puts the explanation in the body instead of the subject. duplication_pct (1.45%) scanned 169 production files; DUPLICATE_IGNORE_PATTERNS (**/designs/**) matches nothing in git.git.

observations.short_count_explanation: commits_analyzed is 49, one short of MAX_COMMITS (50). Unlike emberjs/ember.js's 49-commit window above (a reproducible, deterministic tool defect: code-quality-metrics-p4c), this shortfall is NOT reproducible: re-cloning curl/curl at this exact repo_head and re-running the identical tool_commit (fcc40d93) against the identical --since window twice on 2026-08-19 produced 50 commits analyzed both times, no warning, no drop -- spanning the identical committer-date range recorded in this observation's window.actual_span (2026-04-22 to 2026-05-15), confirming the same 50-commit window is selected both times and exactly one commit within it failed to be scored the first time. The most plausible explanation is a third instance of the transient blobless-fetch defect already recorded twice in this dataset: microsoft/playwright's 49-commit window (98769e38, this file's squash-merge population), whose notes quote the literal warning ('No stats found for commit'), and -- per that same observation's notes -- django/django's 2026-03-02 window. All three windows were cloned with this project's prescribed `--filter=blob:none --single-branch` recipe (calibration/README.md, 'Adding a repository'), under which `git show --numstat` on a commit whose blob was not yet locally fetched can fail against the clone's promisor remote; that failure is caught by runGitCommand and analyzeCommit drops the commit, printing 'Warning: No stats found for commit <sha>' -- the same code path independently confirmed to fire deterministically for ember.js's genuinely-empty-commit case above, but which a network-timing failure would trigger only sometimes. This record's original run did not preserve the specific warning text (unlike playwright's), so this is the best-supported explanation available rather than a certainty; see commits_analyzed_correction for what a clean 50-commit run of this identical window measures. CORRECTION (code-quality-metrics-jvt8): this explanation described itself as the third instance of the transient blobless-fetch class, on the strength of playwright's record citing a django instance. That django cross-reference does not hold, so this is at most the second instance and the class rests on playwright alone. The direct evidence for this observation is unchanged and still stands: two re-runs at the same pin produced 50 commits cleanly with the exact recorded actual_span, so the same window is selected and one commit within it failed to score, which rules out a deterministic defect. But a class with one other confirmed member is weaker support than a class with two, and the alternative reading, that this value simply cannot be reproduced from its own provenance and should be excluded rather than explained, is not closed off.

commits_analyzed_correction.reason: Recorded for completeness alongside emberjs/ember.js's correction above, using the same method: re-running this observation's own tool_commit (fcc40d93) against the identical pinned repo_head and --since window in a scratch clone. Unlike ember's case this is not a defect fix being isolated -- it is simply a clean re-run of a window whose original run is believed to have dropped one commit to a transient fetch failure.
commits_analyzed_correction.method: Fresh --filter=blob:none --single-branch clone of curl/curl reset to repo_head 614b94ee, tool_commit fcc40d93 run twice with `--since 2026-04-16`; both runs produced 50 commits with these metrics and no warning. duplication_pct is left at its already-recorded, separately re-measured value (see duplication_remeasurement): it is a whole-tree jscpd scan at the checked-out repo_head, not a per-commit aggregate, so it does not depend on which commits were scored.

observations.exclusion_reason: REAL-WORLD ANOMALY, not a tool defect (code-quality-metrics-4cv finding): this repository's second-ever commit by author date is dated 2025-01-24 -- roughly three years after the root commit (2022-01-26, 'Initial commit', a non-empty 123-line/2-file commit, so this is not the same empty-commit defect found in django's observation). The repository was evidently created and then left dormant before real development began. Because windowIncludesRepositoryRoot only checks whether the pinned window's analyzed set includes the structural root -- which it does here, since the root is the sole ancestor of every later commit regardless of the calendar gap -- project_lifecycle self-reports 'initial-build' even though analyzed_span_start/end (2022-01-26 to 2025-01-30) span three years for what is nominally a 50-commit window. This technically passes the consistency check the task asked for (detector and intent agree that the window includes the root) while still not being a usable six-month greenfield window: 49 of the 50 fetched commits (42 analyzed after merge-commit filtering) actually fall within a single week in January 2025, not spread across the nominal span. See the sibling 'kenjudy/73V (post-dormancy comparison)' observation for the corrected window, and the report's discussion of the opposite-direction disagreement it produces.

But because the repository's structural root sits three years earlier and is not among these 50 analyzed commits, project_lifecycle self-reports 'established' rather than 'initial-build' -- the opposite-direction disagreement from django's: here the window IS what was intended as greenfield, but the detector does not confirm it, because the root-inclusion check has no notion of a dormancy gap. Recorded so this disagreement is visible rather than silently resolved either way; the metrics broadly agree in shape with the sibling root-anchored observation above (16% vs 14.29% large commits, 4% vs 4.76% sprawling), which is some evidence the underlying practice being measured is the same regardless of which window is used, even though only one of the two satisfies the tool's own root-inclusion rule.

reservations.concern: Every window was measured in 2026, so these projects may already have adopted AI assistance. This toolkit exists to detect AI drift, and calibrating to a contemporary sample risks defining healthy as whatever drift is already present. UPDATE 2026-08-18: a pre-2022 (2019-2020) baseline has now been measured for all six references (era:pre-ai observations below, 12 windows against the 12 era:current windows). Movement between eras is real but modest for most metrics and mixed in direction -- message_quality_pct and large_commits_pct/avg_lines_changed moved in opposite directions, so this sample does not show uniform AI-era degradation. See the drift-report task notes for the full per-metric movement table.
reservations.implication: Bands describe what these projects do now, not what they did before AI. A pre-2022 window for the same repositories would be a genuinely stronger baseline and is the single most valuable addition to this dataset. The severity is downgraded from high to medium because the baseline this reservation called for now exists and does not show dramatic movement -- but the sample is still only two 50-commit windows per repository per era (24 total), so this qualifies rather than retires the concern.

reservations.concern: All six reference repositories preserve individual commits. They had to: the tool measures commits, and a squash-merge repository yields one commit per pull request, so its numbers describe pull request shape instead of working habits. Roughly twenty one well known projects were rejected on that basis to find six usable, including eslint, prettier, vuejs/core, TypeScript, angular, webpack, babel, react, svelte, jest, express, python/cpython, apache/kafka and kubernetes. Squash merging is the more common workflow, so the reference set is drawn from the minority case. Partially addressed (code-quality-metrics-7sk): a separate squash-merge reference set now exists (python/cpython, apache/kafka, microsoft/playwright, facebook/react, TanStack/query; population: "squash-merge" in observations.json), with its own bands derivable via `derive-bands.js --population squash-merge`. This downgrades the severity from high to medium, the same way the pre-ai-baseline reservation was downgraded once a pre-ai window existed, but does not retire it: the squash-merge set is 5 repositories and 10 included windows against the granular set's 6 repositories and 24, so it is a thinner population and its own bands carry a wider reservation of the same two-windows-per-repo and narrow-population kind. The two populations must never be pooled (selectByPopulation defaults to granular).
reservations.implication: These bands are valid for granular-history repositories, which are the minority. Applied to a squash-merge repository the unit of measurement differs, so it will look worse on every size metric for reasons unrelated to practice. Note also that granular history is not independent of project generation: the six references are predominantly older projects with mailing list or integrator cultures predating the GitHub squash norm, which compounds the narrow-population reservation rather than sitting beside it. Squash repositories need their own reference set and their own bands, and until then their verdicts should be withheld rather than computed. A squash-merge repository can now get a real, if provisional, verdict from the squash-merge bands instead of having every commit-unit verdict withheld -- but that verdict rests on a smaller sample than the granular one, so treat it as more provisional still.

reservations.concern: The repositories were chosen because they are considered disciplined, and healthy is then defined as what they do. Choosing references and reading bands off their quantiles is how a reference benchmark works (it is Alves et al.'s own published procedure), so this is not a circular derivation; but nothing validates the reference choice itself, and if the field as a whole has drifted, the bands calibrate to that drift.
reservations.implication: The bands say a project is no worse than these six, which is a weaker claim than a project is healthy. Reputation is not a measured outcome, so the exposure is an unvalidated reference choice and a small n. (The id 'circular-definition' predates this rewording and is kept for continuity.)

reservations.concern: No defect rate, delivery stability, incident frequency or review depth was measured for any reference repository. The selection rests on reputation and visible commit discipline.
reservations.implication: These bands calibrate to projects believed to work well, not to projects measured to work well. The link from commit shape to delivery outcome remains an inference, and DORA's own outcome data is survey-derived rather than commit-derived.

reservations.concern: All six are mature open-source infrastructure projects with heavy public review cultures, long histories and many contributors. None is a commercial product team, a small team, a greenfield project or a codebase under deadline pressure.
reservations.implication: The population this tool is aimed at, ordinary product teams adopting AI, is not represented. Practice norms in a project like postgres are not obviously the right target for a five person team shipping weekly.

reservations.concern: Every window measures maintenance-era work on a decades-old codebase. No reference repository was measured during an initial build phase, and the tool has no notion of project lifecycle. Note this is a separate axis from era: era distinguishes pre-AI (2019-2020) from current calendar time, while this concerns where a project sits in its own life, and every observation in both eras is brownfield. This narrows the greenfield item already listed under narrow-population to a specific, directional defect: several metrics are biased against greenfield by construction, not merely uncalibrated for it. LARGE_COMMITS_PCT is the clearest case that still carries a verdict. Hattori and Lanza found large commits are disproportionately forward engineering while bug fixes are the smallest commits (EVOL 2008, Section 5.2), and initial build additionally carries scaffolding, vendored dependencies and generated files. P90_LINES_CHANGED inherits the same bias for the same reason. DUPLICATION_PCT is third, on arithmetic rather than published evidence: it divides duplicated lines by total lines, so a young codebase with a small denominator swings on a few blocks. The sharpest illustration is a metric that no longer carries a band: net_additions_ratio_median maps onto Nagappan and Ball's M7, which they defined to detect exactly this, 'In feature development the lines churned is much greater than the lines deleted, so a high value of M7 indicates new feature development' (ICSE 2005, Section 4). It is now reported without a verdict, so it can no longer produce a false alarm, but it remains a reason to read the reported figure with lifecycle in mind. Test co-change is a further candidate, since scaffolding often lands before a test suite exists, but no source was found for it and it is reasoning rather than evidence. Partially addressed (code-quality-metrics-4cv): a greenfield reference set now exists, split into two population values that must never be pooled with each other or with the granular default (population: "greenfield-historical" -- each of emberjs/ember.js, curl/curl, postgres/postgres and nodejs/node measured during its own first ~50 commits; population: "greenfield-modern" -- stride-nyc/remote_retro and stride-nyc/dotnetdependencytracer measured during their own first several months -- so era and lifecycle stay separate axes rather than the greenfield set re-collapsing them the way a historical-only greenfield sample would). This downgrades the severity from high to medium, the same way granular-history-only and pre-ai-baseline were downgraded once their own remedies were measured, but does not retire it: of the nine repositories targeted, only 4 of 6 historical baselines and 2 of 3 modern repositories produced a usable observation. git/git could not be measured in the environment this measurement ran in. django/django's repository root is an empty SVN-import artifact that a lib/git.js defect (analyzeCommit treats an empty diff identically to a git-command failure) silently drops from the analyzed set, so its window cannot self-report initial-build despite structurally reaching the root. kenjudy/73V's repository root sits roughly three years before its real development began, so its root-anchored window passes the structural root-inclusion check while still not being a genuine six-month window. No band from either new population has been adopted into lib/thresholds.js; see calibration/README.md's Greenfield reference set section for the full derivation table, the historical/modern comparison, and whether greenfield duplication_pct is stable enough to band at all.
reservations.implication: A greenfield project in its build phase will read as drifting on several banded metrics while doing nothing wrong, and the direction of every bias is the same: toward a worse verdict. The bands support 'no worse than these six mature projects during maintenance' and should not be applied to an initial build until a greenfield reference set exists. This also qualifies the external comparison recorded for P90_LINES_CHANGED: Kolassa's p90 of 261 pools full project histories across roughly 11,000 projects and therefore includes initial build phases, so it is a mixed-lifecycle population being compared against a brownfield-only band, not a like-for-like check. A greenfield project can now be measured against derive-bands.js's own greenfield-historical or greenfield-modern proposal (once one is reviewed and adopted) instead of only being told 'no worse than these six mature projects during maintenance' -- but both new populations are thinner than even the squash-merge set (4 and 2 usable repositories respectively, one non-repeating window per repository), so any band adopted from them should be treated as more provisional than the granular default's already-qualified bands, not less.

reservations.concern: Two windows cannot establish stability, and within-repository variance is often as large as between-repository variance. nodejs/node measured 5.12 percent and 15.09 percent duplication across its own two windows; git measured 0 percent then 21 of 50 commits touching tests once the t/ pattern was fixed.
reservations.implication: A band whose extreme comes from one window is not evidence, which is why the tiering scheme withholds a critical bound in those cases. More windows per repository would firm this up more cheaply than more repositories.

reservations.concern: MAX_COMMITS is 50, so each observation samples 50 commits. A single vendored dependency sync, translation import or bulk test import can dominate that window, and several were excluded for exactly that reason.
reservations.implication: Excluding unrepresentative windows is a judgement call that narrows the observed range and therefore tightens bands. The exclusions are recorded per observation so the effect is auditable, but they are not neutral.

reservations.concern: The set spans C (git, postgres, curl), C++ and JavaScript (node), JavaScript (ember) and Python (django). Duplication in particular is language sensitive, and DUPLICATE_MIN_LINES 5 with DUPLICATE_MIN_TOKENS 50 are jscpd's stock defaults rather than values chosen for any language here.
reservations.implication: Duplication bands mix populations that may not be comparable. The 5 line minimum does match GitClear's own definition of a duplicate block, which is the one parameter in this toolkit with a primary source behind it.

reservations.concern: Dependency bots contribute real commits with terse generated messages. An ember window with 8 of 49 commits from Renovate set the observed floor for message quality.
reservations.implication: Bot volume varies enormously between projects and is not a property of human practice. Metrics that read commit messages or commit counts are distorted by it, and no filtering is applied.

reservations.concern: Six tool defects were found by measuring rather than by inspection, three of which changed what a metric counts: production-only line counting, repository-root test directory detection, and merge commit exclusion. The first 12 observations are retired for that reason.
reservations.implication: Observations are only valid for the tool commit that produced them, which is recorded per record. Any future fix that changes what a metric counts retires the affected observations again.

reservations.concern: Every observation in this file was measured by a tool build whose commit selection sorted the newest-MAX_COMMITS pick by author date (git %ai), while --since already filters commits by committer date. On a rebase-and-land or cherry-pick workflow the two diverge -- a commit's author date can sit well before its committer date -- so the 'newest 50' the sort picked was not reliably the 50 commits --since would itself call newest. Measured directly: reproducing the recorded nodejs/node observation below (repo_head cb9bb667, since 2026-08-01, tool_commit fcc40d93) gives large_commits_pct 14, matching the recorded value; re-sorting the identical window by author date against current HEAD gave 18 -- a different set of 50 commits selected under the same nominal window (code-quality-metrics-75 / mbiw). The fix (this same change) sources commit.date from %ci (committer date) instead, so selection, analyzed_span_start/end, velocity and trend all key off the same clock --since filters by.
reservations.implication: Every observation recorded before this fix's tool_commit selected commits under author-date sorting and is retired for the same reason measurement-changed-mid-calibration retires the first 12: the commit set a window claims to cover is not reliably the commit set that was actually analyzed. Re-measurement is bundled into the same pass as code-quality-metrics-69 and -62 per issue #75's own notes, rather than run as a separate calibration pass.

reservations.concern: code-quality-metrics-9bj5 (issue #62) turned on default exclusion of dependency/CI bot commits (dependabot, renovate, github-actions, release/version-bump bots, other [bot] accounts) from every metric's denominator, while never excluding a commit attributable to an AI coding agent. This changes what every commit-shape metric counts on any reference repository where such bots contributed commits in the analyzed window -- the bot-traffic reservation above already documents one measured case (an ember window, 8 of 49 commits from Renovate) where bot volume set the observed floor for message quality; with the filter on, that floor no longer exists and every metric computed over that window's denominator would measure differently.
reservations.implication: Every observation recorded before this tool_commit was measured without bot exclusion and is not comparable to a measurement taken after it, independent of the measurement-changed-mid-calibration reservation above (a different tool defect). Re-measuring the six reference repositories at the new setting is tracked as follow-up work, sequenced together with code-quality-metrics-69's vendored/generated exclusion (also observation-invalidating) so both land in one re-measurement campaign rather than two.

reservations.concern: Zhang, Mockus, Zou, Khomh and Hassan ('How Does Context Affect the Distribution of Software Maintainability Metrics?', ICSM 2013, DOI 10.1109/ICSM.2013.46) measured 320 SourceForge systems across 39 metrics and found that every one of six studied context factors (domain, language, age, lifespan, number of changes, number of downloads) shifts metric distributions; language alone shifted 35 of the 39 metrics. The six repositories behind these bands are one context (mature, granular-history, C/C++/JS/Python infrastructure projects with heavy public review cultures), not a population sample.
reservations.implication: A band derived here should not be assumed to hold for a project in a different language, domain, age bracket, or size class. This compounds, rather than duplicates, the narrow-population reservation: that one is about who the six projects are, this one is about the general empirical fact that commit-shape metrics move with context at all.

reservations.concern: Kamei, Fukushima, McIntosh, Yamashita, Ubayashi and Hassan ('Studying just-in-time defect prediction using cross-project models', EMSE 21(5):2072-2106, 2016, DOI 10.1007/s10664-015-9400-x, Table 6) found within-project JIT defect models score 0.74-0.83 AUC on their own project, but the same models applied cross-project on the same eleven projects fall as low as 0.38 AUC -- worse than random. That is a fitted, multi-feature statistical model failing to transfer, and the result bounds fitted prediction models: a benchmark quantile predicts nothing, so it cannot fail by scoring worse than chance, and on a project unlike the references it fails instead by the comparison going uninformative. It remains the clearest published warning against carrying any project-derived number to a dissimilar project.
reservations.implication: Applying these bands to a project unlike the six references is an extrapolation the field's nearest analogue warns against, though the failure mode is an uninformative comparison rather than worse-than-chance prediction. The bands should be read as describing these six projects, not as generalizing to an unseen one, until an outcome-validated transfer test exists.

reservations.concern: McIntosh and Kamei ('Are Fix-Inducing Changes a Moving Target?', TSE 44(5):412-428, 2018, DOI 10.1109/TSE.2017.2693980) found JIT defect models lose 11-34 percentage points of AUC just one year after training, and the explanatory share of the Size family of metrics swings between 10-43% (Qt) and 3-37% (OpenStack) of period-specific importance. A frozen threshold is exactly the artefact this paper warns against: the relationship between a commit-shape metric and whatever it is meant to predict does not hold still even within a single project's own history.
reservations.implication: These bands should be treated as dated to their calibration run (tool_commit and observation date are recorded per record for this reason) and re-derived periodically rather than treated as a permanent constant, even for the same six reference repositories.

reservations_note: These reservations qualify every band derived from this file. They are recorded here rather than in lib/thresholds.js so that the caveats travel with the evidence, and so that adding reference repositories forces a reader to reconsider which reservations still apply.
